props.title: Le Samouraï
props.initialSlug: Hitman's code of honor leads to deadly choices

sections.content: Le Samouraï (1967) revolutionized the hitman genre through Jean-Pierre Melville's masterful minimalism. Alain Delon's ice-cold performance as Jef Costello created the template for every lone assassin character that followed, from The Professional (1994) to Drive (2011). Melville strips away everything unnecessary, leaving only essential elements - the ritualistic preparation, the perfect alibi, the code of honor. The film's influence extends far beyond crime cinema, with directors like John Woo and Jim Jarmusch openly acknowledging its impact on their work, particularly visible in The Killer (1989) and Ghost Dog: The Way of the Samurai (1999).

sections.content: The film's visual language established a new grammar for crime cinema. Melville's use of color, particularly the muted blues and grays of Paris, influenced neo-noir aesthetics for decades. Drive (2011) borrowed heavily from this palette, while The American (2010) practically remade Le Samouraï's methodical pacing and focus on professional ritual. The attention to detail in Costello's meticulous preparation scenes created a template followed by films like John Wick (2014) and Collateral (2004).

Le Samouraï's exploration of solitude and professional ethics spawned countless imitators. The protagonist's spartan apartment and rigid routine influenced characters from Taxi Driver (1976) to Leon (1994). Melville's fusion of Western noir with Eastern philosophy created a new archetype - the philosophical hitman - seen in films like The Limits of Control (2009) and Bangkok Dangerous (2008). sections.content: Contemporary filmmakers continue drawing from Le Samouraï's well. You Were Never Really Here (2017) adopts its elliptical storytelling and protagonist's isolation, while The Man from Nowhere (2010) transposes its aesthetic to South Korean cinema. Even Marvel's Black Widow (2021) borrowed from Le Samouraï's assassination sequences and professional detachment.
